What can be seen from a point

Source: R/viewshed.R
viewshed.Rd

The ground visible from an eye at height eye above the terrain at xy, computed exactly on the terrain as triangles (vertices at cell centres, each square of four split on the diagonal from top-left to bottom-right).

Usage

viewshed(
  z,
  extent = NULL,
  xy,
  eye = 1.5,
  far = NULL,
  far_extent = NULL,
  max_dist = Inf,
  curvature = TRUE,
  supersample = 2L,
  pieces = TRUE,
  sectors = 64L
)

Arguments

z

matrix of heights, row 1 at the north edge, square cells; or the result of gdalraster::read_ds() (a vector with a gis attribute), in which case extent is taken from it

extent

c(xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax) of z

xy

the eye, c(x, y), inside z (inside the hull of its cell centres)

eye

height of the eye above the ground (m)

far, far_extent

optional coarser grid surrounding z (and its extent), for terrain further out; its cells that touch z are skipped

max_dist

ignore terrain further than this (m)

curvature

lower the terrain by d^2 / 2R (earth curvature with standard refraction, k = 0.13)

supersample

visible fraction per cell is sampled at supersample^2 points per cell (0 to skip)

pieces

keep the visible polygons

sectors

sectors per 90 degree wedge (more: less bookkeeping per sector) Missing heights (sea, say) are treated as 0 m for the line of sight, so open water does not block the view, and are missing in visible.

Value

a list with visible (matrix like z, fraction of each cell visible, for ximage::ximage(v$visible, extent = v$extent)), extent, area (includes ground that was missing in z) (visible area, m^2, including far), skyline (data frame of azimuth, degrees clockwise from grid north, and elevation of the horizon, degrees), pieces (data frame of polygon vertices x, y with piece, triangle and ring ids), eye (x, y, z of the eye) and counts. NULL if xy is outside z.

Details

The method is an object-space visibility map. Around the eye, four 90 degree wedges of azimuth each use the central (gnomonic) projection, in which straight edges stay straight. Triangles are visited front to back, and a horizon is kept per narrow sector of azimuth as an upper envelope. A triangle is visible exactly where it rises above the horizon, which it then raises. The visible pieces map back to the ground as convex polygons, and the horizon left at the end is the skyline.

Examples

## volcano, georeferenced (New Zealand Map Grid, EPSG:27200)
z <- volcano[nrow(volcano):1, ncol(volcano):1]
ex <- c(2667400, 2668010, 6478700, 6479570)
v <- viewshed(z, ex, c(2667700, 6478900))
v
#> <aspersions viewshed>
#>   eye at (2667700.0, 6478900.0), height 193.5
#>   visible: 40,660 m^2 from 875 of 10,320 triangles
#>   8.2% of the grid visible
#>   5468 visible pieces
#>   skyline: -8.8 to 12.6 degrees
if (requireNamespace("ximage", quietly = TRUE)) {
  ximage::ximage(z, extent = ex, col = grey.colors(64), asp = 1)
  ximage::ximage(v$visible, extent = ex, add = TRUE,
                 col = c(NA, adjustcolor("gold", 0.7)), breaks = c(-1, 0.01, 2))
}
